correctness.rationale: The triangular graph has two positive Laplacian spectral projectors constructed exactly from the complete-graph point-pair incidence matrix. Their contractions with two edge dipoles are explicitly c_{k,h} and t_{k,h}. Every pair belongs to one of five invariant signatures, and 1-r>|c| proves two-edge removal preserves connectivity and validates the rank-two Woodbury formula. Four rationally factored adjacent differences have strictly positive numerators and denominators for all n>=5. Exhaustive symbolic counts total C(|E|,2). Independent exact grounded-Laplacian inversions verify 15 representatives for n=5,6,7; entire pair-class counts checked n=5..9; finite checks do not constitute the infinite proof.

evidence: A previous exact two-edge Kirchhoff classification on balanced complete multipartite graphs covers the exceptional case T(4)=K_{2,2,2}; that case is not claimed.

originality.rationale: The new theorem is the complete five-class two-edge Kirchhoff-index damage classification of J(n,2), n>=5, including a strict global ranking, exact rational values, and all maximizing-pair counts. This is not implied directly by the inspected published general resistance or edge-outage frameworks, Johnson spectra alone, or previously documented complete-multipartite classifications; the sole triangular complete-multipartite special case n=4 is expressly excluded. A targeted published-finding corpus/public literature search found no equivalent all-n two-fault table. Incompletely indexed specialized work remains a residual risk.

value.rationale: The unweighted triangular graphs are canonical strongly regular line graphs modeling pairwise interactions. Edge transitivity makes all first-link losses equivalent, so it is a substantive robustness question which second-link placements are most damaging. The theorem derives exact damage of every pair, determines a five-class strict ranking that distinguishes triangles from open wedges, and counts all worst simultaneous failures for an infinite network family. This is not an arbitrary small-size table or a mere reuse of a numerical constant; it resolves a complete finite-failure design problem over all n>=5.
